recognise it. That is the verifier's floor from Ottawa, adopted rather than re-derived, because no
blind pass has been run on this subject and the artist does not set the threshold for their own
work. What the size ladder shows as a DRAWING OBSERVATION and explicitly not an identification: at
200 px every mustBeRight feature is still legible, including the two bells and the gold ball.
The two-size test in art-bible section 5 was run at the shipping size of 800 x 1010 and passed at
both probes, which is what ADR-0013 as amended requires before a landmark ships at 1x rather than
the 2x default. The measured saving is 12.32 MiB -> 3.08 MiB of decoded texture.

subjects.subject: The immigration and ocean terminal buildings at Pier 21, Halifax
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswer: a pier shed and an ocean liner
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT IS DELIBERATELY NOT ASKED FOR A PLACE NAME, and the reason is a property of the
building rather than of the drawing. Pier 21 is a brick shed. Its one unmistakable feature in every
photograph is the name PAINTED ON IT, and a round emblem beside the name - and this project draws
no lettering anywhere, for a reason that has nothing to do with this level: make verify-art refuses
any render source containing a <text> element, because a name drawn into the picture defeats every
byte-level leak check in the hand-off. Strip the name and what is left is a three-storey brick
block with a streamlined entrance, which is a building type and not a place.
SO THE GENERIC ANSWERS PASS. `Pier 21` and `Halifax` stay in the list because a verifier who names
them is not wrong - the liner, the terminal block and the immigrant train together are a fair
inference - but they are NOT required, and the gate must not reward them. Ottawa's canal subject
demanded a city name from a tile its own notes forbade putting a city cue on, passed on the
verifier's inference from project context, and had to be amended afterwards. The PO flagged this
one in advance and declined to write an expectedBlindAnswer for it. This is the answer to that:
draw the shed accurately, ask it only for what it can carry, and put the level's place-identity on
`town-clock`, which can.
One answer was removed from this list before it ever ran: "a port terminal". The hand-off's
leak scanner takes single words of four letters or more out of `id` and `expectedBlindAnswer`
and refuses any handed-over text containing one, and the briefing it writes contains the word
"important". `quebec-city-riverfront`'s note states the rule as "no common English word of
four letters or more"; the real rule is narrower and nastier - no word that is a SUBSTRING of
any word in the briefing. Checked mechanically against the real `leakTokens` before shipping.

mustBeRight.feature: a three-storey red brick block with a flat stone-coped parapet
mustBeRight.why: It is the building. Everything else in the frame is context for it.
mustBeRight.detail: Red-brown facing brick with a pale stone coping at the parapet, one stone band below the coping and one string course at mid height, and a rhythm of rectangular sash windows with stone sills, three storeys of them. MEASURED on halifax/pier-21-entrance.jpg, converted to sRGB first: the hue-filtered median of 104302 sunlit brick pixels is #c07e70 = hsl(11,39%,60%). That is a LIGHTER, REDDER brick than the Chateau Frontenac's, whose sunlit median is hsl(29,42%,46%). The shipped art uses the existing `brick` ramp anyway, whose light tone is hsl(25,52%,59%) - the same lightness, 14 degrees more orange. A second near-identical brick ramp was rejected: the two buildings are in different levels and never on screen together, and the palette does not need two reds to say brick. The departure is recorded here rather than hidden.

mustBeRight.feature: a pale streamlined entrance standing proud of the brick
mustBeRight.why: It is the one piece of architecture on the building that is not a shed, and it is what dates it. Without it the block is a warehouse.
mustBeRight.detail: A pale rendered pylon with rounded corners, a curved cantilevered canopy over the doorway and a small balcony with a plain pipe rail above it. Drawn from halifax/pier-21-entrance.jpg. NOT a classical portico, NOT columns.

mustBeRight.feature: long low pier sheds running away on both sides
mustBeRight.why: A terminal is a shed with a small building attached, not a building on its own, and the length is the whole character of the place.
mustBeRight.detail: Two-storey sheds with shallow roofs carrying a raised monitor along the ridge, a rhythm of small windows, and walls markedly paler than the brick. They run off both edges of the frame: the real shed is over 350 m long and nothing in a portrait frame can show that except by leaving.

mustBeRight.feature: an ocean liner berthed alongside, rising above the shed roof
mustBeRight.why: The ship is what a pier shed is FOR, and it is the difference between this render and a row of warehouses. halifax/pier-21-liner-1934.jpg shows exactly this: a three-funnelled liner alongside the shed, taller than everything on the pier.
mustBeRight.detail: A dark hull with a red boot band, a white superstructure with window bands and a row of boats along the boat deck, two buff funnels with dark tops, and one plain mast. Generic: no line's livery, no name, no house flag. Two funnels rather than three - the count may differ from the photograph, the massing may not.

mustBeRight.feature: a railway coach standing on a track in front of the building
mustBeRight.why: People who arrived here left by train, and the track runs along the pier apron in every reference. It is drawn because halifax/pier-21-entrance.jpg shows a preserved coach standing exactly there, not because a train would be a nice idea.
mustBeRight.detail: A dark green heritage passenger coach on rails and sleepers, with a window rhythm, a brass stripe under the windows and two trucks. No lettering, no number, no reporting mark.

simplifyAway: brick coursing and mortar joints
window glazing bars: one dark pane with one horizontal bar
the fire escapes, downpipes, roof vents and modern plant on the shed roofs
the parapet's brick corbelling and the moulded stone profiles: each becomes one flat band
the coach's underframe detail, couplers, steps and roof vents
neverAdd: the painted name on the parapet, in any size or language, or any other lettering anywhere in the level. It is what the building is known by and it is the one thing this project cannot draw

the round emblem beside the name on the brick face: it is the operating institution's mark, and an approximated mark is worse than none - the same reasoning art-bible section 10 applies to the officer's insignia
a clock face on this building. There is no clock here; the round sign is a sign, and drawing it as a clock would make this landmark and Ottawa's and Halifax's own Town Clock all the same landmark
a flag, a coat of arms or a house flag on the liner
a lighthouse, a fort or a bridge in the same frame: none of them is at Pier 21
notes: halifax/pier-21-entrance.jpg is CC BY 3.0 and is the primary reference for the brick block, the
streamlined entrance, the stone banding and the coach. It is an oblique view, so it is a reference
for elements and colour and NOT for a width-to-height ratio.
halifax/pier-21-liner-1934.jpg is public domain, is an aerial, and is the reference for the shed's
length, the liner alongside and the covered gangway. It is also the only reference showing what the
place was built to do.
halifax/pier-21-and-the-seaport.jpg is public domain, small and low contrast. It is here for one
thing: it shows how completely the painted name carries the building's identity, which is the
finding this subject's expectedBlindAnswerNote rests on.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: 300 px wide, adopted from Ottawa as above. The shipped source is 900 x 620.

subjects.subject: A timber harbour boardwalk running past working wharves
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the town above the quayside, the quayside placed 160 px below the town tile's top edge (world y 860 against 700). Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1800 and 2016) rather than laying them side by side, and draw the quayside over the town where they overlap, which is the order the level uses. Neither file answers the subject alone: a town with no waterfront is a town, and a boardwalk with nothing behind it is a fence. `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'uptown', nearMatch: 'quayside', nearTop: 160 })`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. Both renders are REPEATING parallax tiles - 1800 px and 2016 px - so a unique
landmark drawn on either appears three or four times across the level. Nothing on them may name a
city, and it follows that nothing may be DEMANDED of them that names one. No answer in this list
names Halifax, Nova Scotia, the Citadel or Pier 21, and a verifier who does name one of them is
not wrong - they are just not required to, and the gate must not reward it.
WHERE HALIFAX ACTUALLY COMES FROM: `town-clock`, a separate non-repeating POI hero that IS
required to be named. The boardwalk is where the player walks; the clock is what says which city.

mustBeRight.feature: a planked timber deck with a low kerb at the water's edge
mustBeRight.why: It is a BOARDWALK, not a quay and not a street. The planking and the timber edge are the whole read, exactly as the built edges are what make Ottawa's ice a canal rather than a pond.
mustBeRight.detail: The boards run ACROSS the view, so the lines between them are horizontal. They were drawn as vertical separators for one composite and read as a picket fence, and then as horizontal hairlines on a flat grey field and read as a PAVED STREET - a blind pass called the composite a waterfront main street and reached no accepted answer. Both failures came from this line, so it now says what makes a deck read as a deck rather than what colour it is. FOUR THINGS, all of them required. (1) Board courses of graded depth, the nearer ones taller, none thinner than 12 px, separated by a dark gap and a lit chamfer on the near board - the gaps between the boards are the strongest lines on the deck. (2) BOARD ENDS: butt joints at a regular period, staggered between courses, thin and quiet - drawn at the weight of the gaps they turn the deck into a brick wall. (3) Enough tone difference between adjacent boards to read as timber rather than as a poured surface, and warm: weathered timber is a warm grey-tan, and the `path` ramp alone is concrete. Author the deck from `stone-light` with `path-light` and `stone-base` boards through it and `path-shade` in the gaps. (4) A visible deck edge: a low timber kerb along the far edge with a lighter sunlit top, a dark underside so it stands proud of the deck, its cast shadow on the deck below it, and the deck's own shadow on the water in the open slips.

mustBeRight.feature: ornate dark lamp standards, bollards and benches along the water's edge
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes the deck a public promenade rather than a working pier, and it is the strongest built rhythm on these tiles.
mustBeRight.detail: Tall dark posts with a single white globe, drawn from halifax/waterfront-boardwalk.jpg; squat rounded mooring bollards; timber benches with dark ends. Everything the boardwalk carries stands at the FAR edge, so the deck nearest the camera stays clear for the player.

mustBeRight.feature: open slips of water between the wharves, with moored hulls
mustBeRight.why: Half of a working waterfront is the water between the wharves, and a boardwalk with no water in the frame is a street.
mustBeRight.detail: Short bands of harbour water between the buildings, with a moored sailing hull and masts, and a tug with a dark hull and a white wheelhouse. Generic: no name, no livery, no house flag.

mustBeRight.feature: low waterfront buildings with steep gables and dormers
mustBeRight.detail: Two- and three-storey buildings with steep pitched roofs, dormer rhythm and shopfronts at the foot, plus one timber cargo shed with big doors and a monitor roof. Rhythm, not count.

mustBeRight.feature: people walking, to the same cartoon proportions as every other character
mustBeRight.why: CLAUDE.md requires identical cartoon proportions for every character, and background figures in a parallax tile are where that rule is quietly broken first.
mustBeRight.detail: Six heads tall, the same proportion canon as the player, drawn small because they stand further from the camera and never because they matter less. Summer clothes. No outline: a figure authored into a parallax tile is background. NO CULTURAL MARKER OF ANY KIND on any of them - docs/content-review.md 3.3 outcome 2, applied deliberately rather than by omission.

mustBeRight.feature: gulls
mustBeRight.detail: A few white gulls on the bollards and in the air. Small, flat, two tones and a beak. They are the one thing on these tiles that says salt water rather than river.

simplifyAway: individual planks below 12 px. AMENDED 2026-09-08: this used to end "and every plank end", and the board ends are now REQUIRED by the first `mustBeRight` entry. A deck with no board ends is a floor of infinitely long planks, which is what a poured surface looks like
the pile cribbing under the deck: it is below the level's ground line and is never drawn
rigging, shrouds and sails on the moored hulls: a mast and one crosstree is the rhythm
faces on the background figures below 12 px
street furniture above the lamp line
neverAdd: any named or recognisable building drawn into either of these two REPEATING tiles. Scoped deliberately: the Town Clock is required on the town-clock subject and forbidden here, and the reason is the tiling, not the building
any lettering, signage or wordmark, in either language
a lighthouse: Peggy's Cove is not in Halifax and is not this level
snow, ice or bare winter trees: this level is summer, and two of this game's other levels are already winter
mountains on the horizon
notes: halifax/waterfront-boardwalk.jpg is CC BY 2.0 and is the primary composition reference: the deck,
the lamps, the benches, the bollards and the interpretive panel in one frame. It is heavily
processed - dark, high contrast, a storm sky - so it is a reference for GEOMETRY only and never
for colour.
halifax/waterfront-and-skyline.jpg and halifax/waterfront-harbour.jpg are CC0 and are the colour
and massing references: the timber wharves, the low waterfront buildings, the slips and the town
rising behind them.
BLIND PASS, 2026-09-08. This subject FAILED. Every `mustBeRight` feature was drawn and none of
`neverAdd` was present; the identifier read the composite as a small coastal town's waterfront main
street and reached none of the seven accepted answers. The single cause was the DECK: a flat grey
field with three hairline separators, no board ends, no visible edge. The cause was in this contract
and not in the drawing - `grey weathered planking` is a true description of a boardwalk and also a
true description of a pavement, and the drawing obeyed it. The first `mustBeRight` entry above now
describes the structure instead, and the deck is redrawn to it: graded board courses, staggered butt
joints on a 336 px period that tiles at the 2016 px seam with the straddling board given one tone at
both ends, warm board-to-board tone variation, and a modelled timber edge with its shadow on the deck
and on the water. Nothing else on the tile changed: no landmark was added and none may be, for the
reason in `expectedBlindAnswerNote`. Judged by rendering the composite and looking at it, three times,
not by reading the SVG.

subjects.subject: The CN Tower, Toronto
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is the POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: ALLOWED to demand a place name, on the same test `chateau-frontenac` passes: a single
non-repeating POI hero drawing one specific structure. It is the only thing in the Toronto level
that names a city - `toronto-trail` is two repeating tiles and is generic on purpose.

mustBeRight.feature: one wide observation pod about three fifths of the way up a very slender shaft
mustBeRight.why: The composition, and the thing that makes this a tower and not a mast. The maskRegion below exists to put a number on how much of the identification it carries.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on toronto/cn-tower-skyline-elevation.jpg (1600x1012) by thresholding the tower against the sky row by row. EVERY FIGURE IS IN MAIN POD WIDTHS, not in fractions of the total height, and that is deliberate: the tower's base is hidden behind the waterfront in this view and in every other reference here, so a ratio against the total height would have an unmeasured denominator - the mistake ADR-0014 records for the Chateau, in a different disguise. Pod maximum width 45 px at row 402. Shaft immediately below the pod 14 px, so SHAFT : POD = 1 : 3.2. Mast tip at row 207, so tip to pod centre = 195 = 4.33 pod widths. Shaft at row 554 is 18 px and the base flare begins about row 640, 5.3 pod widths below the pod centre. The shipped art is a 97 px pod with a 29 px shaft (1 : 3.3), 4.33 pod widths of mast, and the flare at 5.3. Anything with a shaft thicker than 1 : 2.5 stops being this tower.
mustBeRight.whyMasked: MEASURED against the shipped 700x1020 render: this rectangle covers the whole observation pod - the deck ring, both dark glass bands and the white radome - and leaves the mast, the smaller upper pod, the shaft, the splayed base, the domed stadium and the glazed block untouched. DIAGNOSTIC, never gating. The Chateau's masked probe dropped 0.80 to 0.35 and the Peace Tower's only 0.92 to 0.80, and the difference told us the Chateau identifies by ensemble and the Peace Tower by two hard tokens. This subject looks like a two-token one - the pod and the dome at its foot - and the mask is how that gets checked instead of assumed.

mustBeRight.feature: the pod's widest element is a fat white ring below its glass bands
mustBeRight.why: It is the single most distinctive thing about the pod and it is what a cartoon flattens away first, leaving a plain disc on a stick.
mustBeRight.detail: From top to bottom: a pale metal deck ring, a dark glass band, a pale ring, a second dark glass band, then a WHITE torus that is wider than all of them, then a dark under-deck. Drawn from toronto/cn-tower-pod.jpg.

mustBeRight.feature: a second, much smaller pod higher up the shaft
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED: at row 310 the shaft widens to 16 px against the main pod's 45, so the upper pod is 0.36 of the main pod's width, and it sits 2.04 pod widths above the main pod's centre. It is small and it is not optional: without it the tower is a single-pod tower, which is a different building.

mustBeRight.feature: a long tapering antenna mast above the pod
mustBeRight.detail: About four pod widths of mast above the pod centre, tapering to a point. DELIBERATE EXAGGERATION, and the only one on this subject: in the best reference here the mast is TWO TO THREE PIXELS wide, at the resolution limit of the photograph, which is 5 px at the size shipped and gone at the 25 per cent probe. It is drawn at 0.155 of the pod width at its base and 0.06 at the tip. Exaggerating an identifying feature is simplification (art-bible 5.2); adding one is invention.

mustBeRight.feature: a tapered concrete shaft that splays into legs at its foot
mustBeRight.detail: Warm pale grey concrete, not steel and not glass. The shaft is a hexagonal prism in life; in elevation it reads as one tapering mass with two darker vertical strips for the ribs. At the bottom it splays out into legs - it is not a cylinder standing on the ground.

mustBeRight.feature: a low white domed stadium at the tower's foot
mustBeRight.why: CONTEXT, drawn because it is really there and is in front of the tower from the water in every wide reference here, and because it is what separates this render from a generic concrete communications tower. The same role Centre Block's wings play for the Peace Tower.
mustBeRight.detail: A shallow white dome on a low ring wall, its top about a sixth of the tower's height, standing in FRONT of the tower's base and hiding part of it. Its width is about a third of the tower's height. No roof panel joints, no retractable roof segments, no lettering.

simplifyAway: the external elevator tracks and their glass fronts
the pod's coloured architectural lighting and any red band: it is programmable and changes nightly, so drawing one state asserts a state
the glass floor and the outdoor walk platform
the third rib of the shaft: two shaded strips read as a ribbed shaft, three read as noise
aerials, dishes and the plant on the mast
the stadium's roof panel joints, its hotel windows and its ring-wall structure below 12 px
neverAdd: lattice steelwork or guy wires: it is a free-standing reinforced concrete tower and drawing it as a guyed lattice mast is the single most likely wrong simplification
a second observation pod at the same level, a crown, a spire or a dome ON THE TOWER
a revolving restaurant sign, a wordmark or any lettering anywhere in the level
a flag on the mast
a clock face: there is no clock, and this game already has two clock towers
notes: toronto/cn-tower-skyline-elevation.jpg is CC0, is the PRIMARY reference and is the only one
measured: a long-distance view from the islands, so it is near-orthographic and the whole tower is
in frame. Its base is hidden behind the waterfront, which is why every ratio here is against the
pod's width rather than against the total height.
toronto/cn-tower-pod.jpg is CC BY 3.0 and is the reference for the pod's bands and the radome.
It is a close view from below, so it is a reference for the band ORDER and nothing else.
toronto/cn-tower-shaft.jpg is CC0, is an extreme worm's-eye view, and is here for the concrete's
colour and the ribbed shaft. It is useless for any proportion at all.
toronto/skyline-overcast.jpg is CC0 and shows the tower small against a flat overcast sky, which
is the closest thing here to how it reads at the size ladder's lower rungs.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: 300 px wide, adopted from Ottawa. The shipped source is 700 x 1020, and the tower
itself is 97 px wide at its widest - so the floor is about the FILE, not the shaft, and a level
that scales this landmark down loses the upper pod first and the mast second.
The two-size test was run at the shipping size and passed at both probes: at 25 per cent the pod,
the upper pod, the mast and the dome all survive, and the 120 px silhouette is a needle with one
bulge and a dome at its foot.

subjects.subject: A separated cycling path along a city waterfront, under a downtown skyline
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the skyline above the boulevard, the boulevard placed 340 px below the skyline tile's top edge (world y 900 against 560). Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1800 and 1440), and draw the boulevard over the skyline where they overlap. Neither file answers the subject alone: a skyline with no street is a skyline, and a path with nothing behind it is a path. `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'skyline', nearMatch: 'boulevard', nearTop: 340 })`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: AMENDED 2026-09-08, and the amendment is two words long. A blind pass answered "a generic modern
city street with a protected bicycle lane" and FAILED, because every accepted form of the word was
a contraction - bike, cycle, cycle track - and none was `bicycle`. The art was not at fault: every
`mustBeRight` entry was found on the tile and the answer describes what is drawn. So `a bicycle lane`
and `a protected bicycle lane` now pass. `protected` is accepted because the separation IS drawn and
is a `mustBeRight` entry of its own - a verifier who names it has seen more of the tile, not less.
This is the same amendment `rideau-canal-skateway` needed and it was found the same way, so state the
general rule once: an `expectedBlindAnswer` list is a VOCABULARY for one picture, and a list that
omits the plain word for the thing drawn measures the verifier's diction rather than the art. It is
widened to the honest answer and no further - nothing here accepts a footpath, a road or a pavement.
GENERIC ON PURPOSE, and this one has teeth: the skyline tile is the layer the LOW preset keeps,
so it is the most-seen art in the level, and it is precisely the layer that may not carry a
recognisable building. Every tower on it is a plain mass. A verifier who names Toronto from these
two tiles would be reporting a defect, not a pass.
WHERE TORONTO ACTUALLY COMES FROM: `cn-tower`, a separate non-repeating POI hero. The trail is
where the player rides; the tower is what says which city.

mustBeRight.feature: an asphalt path carrying a green line and a blue line along its length
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes the path a signed cycling route rather than a footpath, and the paired coloured lines are the strongest single piece of built character on these tiles.
mustBeRight.detail: Two flat longitudinal stripes, one green and one blue, running the full width of the tile, drawn from toronto/waterfront-trail.jpg where they run the length of the waterfront path. Straight, level and parallel.

mustBeRight.feature: a white bicycle mark and a direction arrow painted on the surface
mustBeRight.why: It is what says BIKE rather than footpath, and it is the only symbol in the level.
mustBeRight.detail: Two wheels, a frame, bars and a saddle, flat white, drawn as shapes from toronto/bike-lane-street.jpg. A road marking, not a sign. There is no lettering anywhere in this level.

mustBeRight.feature: a planted verge and a kerb separating the path from the road
mustBeRight.why: The separation is the whole point of the facility, and a lane painted at the edge of traffic is a different and more dangerous thing to depict.
mustBeRight.detail: A strip of grass with a sunlit top edge and a pale kerb along the far side of the path.

mustBeRight.feature: young street trees, slim rather than mature
mustBeRight.detail: Recent plantings about twice head height with a narrow canopy, not a spreading avenue tree. toronto/waterfront-trail.jpg shows exactly this: thin trunks in a grass strip. Drawing them as mature maples would put the path in a park.

mustBeRight.feature: people riding, to the same cartoon proportions as every other character
mustBeRight.why: CLAUDE.md requires identical cartoon proportions for every character, and background figures in a parallax tile are where that rule is quietly broken first.
mustBeRight.detail: Six heads tall, the same proportion canon as the player, drawn small because they are across the path. Helmets rather than hairstyles, because the level's locomotion is a bike. No outline. NO CULTURAL MARKER OF ANY KIND - docs/content-review.md 3.3 outcome 2.

mustBeRight.feature: a dense downtown skyline of tall towers behind
mustBeRight.detail: Plain rectangular masses in pale concrete, dark glass and blue-green glass, with flat tops, crowns, setbacks and plant enclosures, standing out of an opaque haze band. Rhythm and massing only.

simplifyAway: individual windows on the towers: a horizontal band rhythm, never a grid of panes
traffic signals, hydro poles and overhead wires
parked cars and moving traffic
the bike-share operator's livery on the bicycles in the rack: they are drawn in palette colours and carry no operator colour and no dock branding
kerb ramps, drainage and tactile paving
neverAdd: any named or recognisable building drawn into either of these two REPEATING tiles, and the CN Tower above all: it is required on the cn-tower subject and forbidden here, and the reason is the tiling, not the building
any lettering, signage or wordmark, in either language
a streetcar, a bus or a train in the cycling lane
mountains on the horizon: this city is on a lake plain
snow or winter trees: this level is late summer
notes: toronto/waterfront-trail.jpg is CC0 and is the primary reference: the separated path, the green
and blue lines, the grass verge, the young trees and the bike rack in one frame.
toronto/bike-lane-street.jpg is CC BY 2.0, from the Ontario government, and is the reference for
the green surface treatment, the white bicycle mark and the arrow. Its required credit line is in
the `author` field of its entry in assets/credits.json, which is where a licence condition of that
kind has to live: credits.schema.json is additionalProperties:false and has no other field for it.
toronto/skyline-overcast.jpg is CC0 and is the massing reference for the tower rhythm.

licenceAudit.method: Wikimedia Commons API, prop=imageinfo&iiprop=extmetadata, before download
licenceAudit.note: Recorded here rather than per asset because credits.schema.json is additionalProperties:false and has no field for a licence-check date. The accepted set widened on 2026-09-08 when the architect reconciled the credits enum with ADR-0004 in both directions: public-domain and CC BY 1.0/2.0/2.5/3.0 added, CC-BY-SA-4.0 removed. Three of the six references parked under OQ-ART-06 became fetchable and are now in; the other three are ShareAlike and stay out. See assets/refs/README.md. Re-run 2026-09-08 for the ten Quebec City references, by the same method and before any of them was downloaded: seven CC0, one public domain (copyright expired, BAnQ), one CC BY 2.0 (Library and Archives Canada) and one CC BY 3.0. Every one is inside the accepted set above. Three ShareAlike candidates that were better photographs - the Dufferin Terrace ice slide in use, the terrace kiosks in winter, and the Chateau after freezing rain - were rejected on licence, not on quality, exactly as three were for Ottawa. Re-run 2026-09-08 for the fifteen Halifax and Toronto references, by the same method and before any of them was downloaded: five CC0, five public domain, three CC BY 2.0, two CC BY 3.0 and one CC BY 4.0. Every one is inside the accepted set above. The Halifax Town Clock's best photographs and every photograph of the Citadel are CC BY-SA and were rejected on licence, not on quality, for the third level running - and for the Town Clock that cost real quality, because the ShareAlike set includes the only high-resolution near-orthographic elevations. The one CC BY 4.0 file that was available carried the day.
